source_document.body:
For much of the past few years, industrial tenants had the luxury of time. Options were plentiful, negotiations dragged and “let’s see what else is out there” was a viable strategy. That window is narrowing.
In a recent market update conversation with Thomas Wasson, Brandon Page , executive vice president and head of leasing and customer solutions at Link Logistics , described a market where demand is building, competition for space is returning and the criteria that decide a lease are shifting. Link Logistics is one of the largest owners and operators of last-mile industrial real estate in North America, with nearly 500 million square feet across the U.S. and Canada. Page oversees portfolio leasing strategy and works closely with its largest customers, which gives him a front-row view of what occupiers want.
For carriers, 3PLs, shippers and anyone else whose network depends on where buildings sit and how they perform, his read is worth a close look.
Demand Is Broadening
Page said demand has built steadily for months. “I would say demand has consistently accelerated throughout the year,” he said, adding that the momentum began toward the end of last year and has continued.
He sorted the drivers into tiers. The most dominant is the AI data center ecosystem, which generates activity during construction and again during ongoing maintenance, alongside advanced manufacturing and reshoring investments that are starting to come online. “We want to own the buildings that are adjacent to [the data centers] to help support those facilities,”Page said.
The second tier is the bread-and-butter freight demand: e-commerce and omnichannel distribution, which follows the consumer and the push toward same-day and next-day delivery. Third-party logistics providers, historically Link Logistics’ largest occupiers, continue to move steadily. Page also pointed to cold storage and to defense and aerospace as specialty segments with new momentum, citing a recently announced Anduril investment likely to affect markets such as Baltimore.
Fast Movers Win
Even as demand builds, Page said tenant decision-making is still deliberate. Customers and their brokers take time to understand a facility and all of its costs. But the dynamics are changing. “We are starting to see situations where we have multiple customers and prospects going after the same building,” he said, noting it’s something Link Logistics saw regularly during COVID.
The implication for occupiers is clear. “Those that are moving quicker are having better success than those that are sort of paralysis by analysis,” Page said.
That message extends to the brokers who represent those tenants. The market remains fairly balanced, he said, but there are more tailwinds than headwinds for landlords heading into year-end than a year ago. Brokers need to prepare clients for rents that will change as markets tighten. “The days of having five or 10 options in a market are gone, and they may have one or two,” he said.
Data Centers Move From Footnote to Force
A couple of years ago, data center-related leasing was a very small part of Link Logistics’ activity. Now it’s a meaningful share. “15% of Link’s new leasing activity over the past year is tied to data centers,” Page said.
He offered a rule of thumb for the scale of the spillover. “Each gigawatt of data center capacity generates roughly 2 million feet,” he said. “We actually think in some cases it’s closer to 2.5 million feet of associated demand.”
Just as important for landlords is how long that demand lasts. Page said 80% of data center-driven demand is long term, with tenants that help stand up facilities and then stay on for ongoing maintenance. The other 20% sign two- to three-year leases focused on setup. “Which is a good tailwind as well for industrial,” he said.
Balancing Scale and Proximity
Two trends in building size can look contradictory but reflect the same goal of efficiency. For large users, Page described “a clear trend of consolidating those 200,000 to 400,000 square foot buildings,” sometimes folding two or three of them into a single facility of about 1 million square feet. Running three buildings means three sets of capital investment and management teams, he said, “just three times the work.” Class A buildings, with their cubic efficiency, tend to lease first.
For last-mile and omnichannel users, the equation flips toward proximity. Link Logistics’ portfolio is largely multi-tenant infill space close to customers, and in those cases, Page said, location can matter more than state-of-the-art specs. “You can’t beat location and access,” he said. Big retail customers are working to get as close to consumers as possible, sometimes delivering in as little as 30 minutes. Whether an order ships from a store or a warehouse, he said, the answer is increasingly “all the above.”
3PLs play a particular role in this environment. Page called them “the fastest way to stand up or modify your national supply chain network,” with less capital tied up than a company standing up its own facility. Large national 3PLs can reposition their portfolios as client needs change.
The New First Question: How Much Power?
If one shift stood out from Link Logistics’ customer advisory council, a roughly 15-member group of the heads of real estate at some of its largest occupiers, it was power. Page said the traditional priority list once ran labor, transportation costs, then rent. Today, “clearly power is the number one driver.”
The numbers show why. A 400,000-square-foot building once came with a 2,000-amp panel. “The new baseline is roughly 4,000 amps,” Page said. Tenants may not use it all on day one, but they’re planning for fleet electrification, extensive material handling and robotics.
The key, he said, is that tenants don’t necessarily need the power immediately. “They don’t necessarily need to have power today, but they need to have a path to power.” They want to know how much capacity is possible and how long it will take to get there, whether six, 12 or 18 months, so they can use other facilities in their network to compensate in the meantime.
Page said some searches now open with the question before any other building attribute is discussed. “‘How much power does it have?’ is line item one,” he said. Square footage and location follow.
Automation: Talked About More Than Deployed
For all the attention on warehouse robotics, Page offered a reality check. “Less than 5% of our facilities actually have automation in there,” he said. Only a handful of Fortune 100 companies can afford the infrastructure and also have the volume to justify it. Costs are falling and systems are becoming more modular, but “it’s still very cost prohibitive for many customers at this point.”
Perception of utilization varies, too. One customer may call a 40-foot-clear building full when product is floor-stacked, while another operating multiple levels of material handling may call itself 90% utilized. It depends, Page said, on the business, the throughput and the technology investment.
Deal Flags: Credit, Term and Flexibility
Asked about red and green flags in closing a deal, Page started with a short rule. “Credit’s king,” he said. A building’s value is tied to the underlying credit and the quality of the rent stream, and short terms on a building that takes significant time to stand up are another warning sign. On the positive side, he points to good-credit tenants investing real capital in a facility, which signals it’s a key part of their network and likely to stay.
For tenants, especially smaller companies where rent is a bigger share of total cost, Page cautioned against focusing only on the face rate. They should ask what capital improvements may be needed and whether the owner can accommodate change. An owner with 50 buildings in a market can offer more room to grow or relocate than one with a single facility. “Make sure you’re partnering with somebody that’s flexible,” he said.
The growth of smaller e-commerce brands and shifts such as the Amazon–UPS breakup on small parcels may also create openings for local and regional 3PLs, Page said.
What to Watch Next
Looking out six to 12 months, Page flagged two open questions. The first is data centers: the election outcome may change sentiment in certain markets, and it remains to be seen how investment from large data center companies plays out. The second is the consumer. Warehouse occupiers aren’t as exposed to interest rates as homebuyers are, he noted, so employment and the underlying health of the economy matter most. When people are employed, they buy more, and Link Logistics’ customers take more space to deliver it efficiently.
That dynamic, Page said, becomes a flywheel as one retailer’s gains force others to follow, “a race to speed,” in his words, that means “you just have to be in a lot more locations and as close to the customers you possibly can get.”
For freight and logistics leaders, the takeaway is practical. Evaluate sites earlier, ask about power first and be ready to decide faster, because the other tenant may already be touring the building.
